candidates.title: Schedule vocabulary review items

demandEvidence.chore: Identify when a learner mistakes an inflected word and assign that vocabulary item a later review date.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: But if you make the mistake of using "play" instead of "played" they're not able to identify that as a component that should have its own schedule for review.

experimentPlan.output: Return a proposed review date and short reason for a learner-supplied word correction.
experimentPlan.trigger: When a learner submits a corrected practice sentence.
steps: Compare original and corrected word forms.
Ask a language model to identify the changed word.
Show a suggested review date using the supplied interval.
Have a tutor confirm the word and date.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a fixed fictional set, verify the changed token matches the known correction and the date follows the chosen interval.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A tutor supplies and approves corrections; the prototype does not diagnose language errors or send real reminders.
unverified: Reliable identification of inflected forms across languages is unverified.
No learning app, learner-data input, reminder delivery, or effectiveness evidence is supplied.

ease.reason: A beginner could test a supplied word pair and review-date suggestion; the post gives no implementation reference.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: language tutors may value review scheduling; this single post does not establish buyer intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week prototype can suggest review dates for fictional word pairs; learner-data ingestion and learning effectiveness are unknown.

autonomy.reason: Suggestions can repeat on supplied examples, but a person must check the correction and manage actual study reminders.

evidence.reason: The post identifies a specific inflection and review-scheduling gap, but frequency and wider demand are uncorroborated.

candidates.reason: Concrete but single-instance learning issue; provisional mean 4.6 is below threshold.

candidates.title: Track an app review follow-up

demandEvidence.chore: Prepare a concise status summary and follow-up draft for an app review that has had no update.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: It has been in “Review process started” status for 55 days, and we haven’t had any updates.

experimentPlan.output: Draft a factual follow-up note from an operator-entered app review status and date.
experimentPlan.trigger: When an app developer records that a review has stalled.
steps: Check that the status and dates are present.
Calculate elapsed days from the supplied dates.
Draft a neutral request for status or missing requirements.
Ask the operator to verify and send it.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For sample dates, compare the calculated elapsed time and draft against a manually written reference.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: The developer verifies all details and sends any message; no platform account or reviewer contact is accessed.
unverified: No review-platform status integration or response-time policy is documented.
The source describes one stalled review, not a recurring paid workflow.

ease.reason: A supplied status can be turned into a draft manually, but no implementation reference supports platform access.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: app developers might value review follow-up help; one complaint shows no paying demand.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can prepare a status note from operator-entered dates; automated status checking is unsupported.

autonomy.reason: The proposed output is a one-time draft from manual inputs, not a repeatable autonomous monitoring loop.

evidence.reason: The retained context states a specific review status and delay, but gives no corroboration or general frequency.

candidates.reason: A narrow note-drafting mock is possible, but the source is a single platform-specific delay; provisional mean 3.8 is below threshold.

candidates.title: Review pages before adding them

demandEvidence.chore: Produce a keep-or-remove review note for a page using its stated purpose and upkeep cost.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Before adding anything new I check whether the page already has a reason to exist. If it does not answer a question or solve something, I delete it.

experimentPlan.output: Create a short page review note that states its supplied purpose and flags missing purpose for human review.
experimentPlan.trigger: When a site owner considers adding or reviewing a page.
steps: Read the supplied title and purpose.
Check whether the purpose names a question or problem.
Draft a keep, clarify, or review recommendation.
Show the reason and ask a person to decide.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On fictional page records, verify every recommendation cites only supplied purpose text and leaves ambiguous cases for review.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A site owner supplies the data and makes every publish or delete decision; no site crawl is proposed.
unverified: No evidence shows recurring client demand or a standard purpose taxonomy.
Quality of the recommendation on real sites is unknown.

ease.reason: A person can supply a page purpose and receive a draft review note; no implementation reference is attached.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small service firms may pay for site-content cleanup; this tip establishes no buyer or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test can review fictional page descriptions; accurate site inventory and traffic data are outside scope.

autonomy.reason: The proposed tool only drafts a note from supplied text; a person decides and removes pages.

evidence.reason: The post gives a general page-keep/delete heuristic, but no specific client, repeated burden, or corroboration.

candidates.reason: The excerpt is a broad personal heuristic, not a sufficiently evidenced repeated customer chore; provisional mean 3.8 is below threshold.

candidates.title: Organize public app security signals

demandEvidence.chore: Make a source-linked checklist of public security statements for a Shopify app, leaving trust judgments to a human.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I’d appreciate any guidance on how to verify an app’s security before installing it in my store.

experimentPlan.output: Organize operator-supplied public statements into a source-linked checklist without rating an app as secure.
experimentPlan.trigger: When a store operator is considering a listed app.
steps: List each supplied statement and its source URL.
Group statements under operator-chosen topics.
Flag topics with no supplied information.
Ask the operator to verify sources and decide.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: Compare each checklist entry with the supplied excerpt and confirm missing topics are marked unknown.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person retrieves public material and makes the installation decision; the prototype does not certify security.
unverified: No official Shopify security badge criteria or independent security sources are supplied.
Reliable source freshness and completeness are unverified.

ease.reason: A manual checklist mock is possible, but no official criteria or implementation source is supplied.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small store operators may value organized app information; this question does not establish payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week prototype can organize operator-supplied public statements, but source verification and security evaluation remain unsupported.

autonomy.reason: The person must find sources and make the security decision; no automated verification is documented.

evidence.reason: The post clearly asks how to verify app security before installation, but gives no specific method or corroboration.

candidates.reason: The task is concrete, but this proposal cannot determine security and lacks supplied criteria; provisional mean 3.6 is below threshold.

candidates.title: Draft agent recovery checklists

demandEvidence.chore: Turn an operator-described failed agent run into a checklist of recovery and duplicate-action questions.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: But devs need to write checkpointers, recovery logic, and deal with idempotency by theirselves.

experimentPlan.output: Produce a review checklist for a supplied agent failure scenario, including checkpoint and duplicate-action questions.
experimentPlan.trigger: When a developer records a failed agent run for review.
steps: Extract the stated restart point and expected side effects.
List which actions may already have occurred.
Draft checkpoint and duplicate-action questions.
Require a developer to decide and implement recovery.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For fictional scenarios, check that every question maps to supplied facts and no action is marked safe without human review.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: The developer supplies the scenario and owns all code changes and production recovery.
unverified: No agent framework, persistence, checkpoint, or idempotency capability is documented.
The excerpt gives no concrete failure example or evidence of repeated demand.

ease.reason: A checklist can be drafted from a supplied failure description, but no implementation reference supports agent recovery.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: developers building agents may value recovery planning; this discussion does not show purchase intent.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can classify fictional failure cases, while actual checkpoint and retry behavior stays outside scope.

autonomy.reason: A person must implement and test every recovery action; the proposed service does not execute recovery.

evidence.reason: The post names checkpointing, recovery logic, and idempotency as developer work, but frequency and specific cases are absent.

candidates.reason: A checklist is a bounded mock but does not implement recovery; source detail is limited; provisional mean 4.0 is below threshold.

candidates.title: Flag product image crop corrections

demandEvidence.chore: Create a correction queue from supplied product-image notes where a messaging app shows a cropped image.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I wish the image added for a product on the messaging app would default to the full size image and not a cut off square one, have to go in and correct it all the time.

experimentPlan.output: Prepare a review queue identifying product images that an operator says need a full-size replacement.
experimentPlan.trigger: When a seller reviews images prepared for a messaging app.
steps: Read the operator label for each fictional item.
Group items marked cropped.
Attach the supplied replacement reference.
Ask the seller to inspect and make each correction.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a fixed fictional list, confirm only items labeled cropped appear in the queue and each retains its supplied reference.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: The seller supplies labels, inspects image quality, and makes changes in the messaging app.
unverified: No source supports image inspection, messaging-app integration, or changing the default crop.
The post identifies recurring correction but not scale or other buyers.

ease.reason: A person can test a queue from supplied image notes, but no image or messaging integration is supported.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: online sellers may value fewer image corrections; one complaint does not establish buyer demand.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can sort fictional image records, but cannot change messaging-app defaults.

autonomy.reason: The person must inspect and correct each image; no automatic image replacement capability is documented.

evidence.reason: The post explicitly says the crop must be corrected repeatedly, but supplies no count or corroborating cases.

candidates.reason: Repeated manual correction is explicit, but only a manually fed queue is supported; provisional mean 4.2 is below threshold.

candidates.title: Prepare daily hiring alert summaries

demandEvidence.chore: Review a supplied daily job-posting list and prepare a deduplicated alert for a recruiter.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Sharing a simple pattern I use for tracking hiring at target companies. Workflow: Schedule Trigger (daily) → Apify node (“Run an Actor and get dataset”) → IF item count > 0 → Slack.

experimentPlan.output: Prepare a daily summary of new job records from a supplied dataset and mark whether the list is empty.
inputs: Fictional job records with title, company, and URL
experimentPlan.trigger: When an operator provides that day’s job records.
steps: Compare supplied URLs with the prior-seen list.
Keep records matching operator-chosen companies.
Count new records using the documented n8n Summarize Count capability.
Draft a compact alert for human review.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For a fixed fictional dataset, verify new-item count and alert contents against a hand-checked list.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: The operator supplies records and confirms relevance before sending; live job-site retrieval and Slack delivery are excluded.
unverified: The supplied n8n reference (02eb5e542dc08527b0ee2cd8) documents Count and Count Unique only, not job retrieval or delivery.
Deduplication correctness on changing job URLs is unverified.

ease.reason: The retained post describes a daily scheduled dataset check and Slack alert; n8n docs support counting input values only.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: recruiters may pay for concise alerts; this maker workflow is not buyer-demand evidence.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can process supplied fictional postings; live ATS retrieval, actor reliability, and Slack sending are unverified.

autonomy.reason: A repeatable count-and-alert pattern is described, and the supplied Summarize reference supports counting; source retrieval and alert delivery still need a person.

evidence.reason: The maker post documents a concrete daily alert workflow and attributed deduplication behavior, but not independent demand.

candidates.reason: The reference supports counting only; the small supplied-data alert is plausible but buyer demand and data retrieval are unproven; provisional mean 4.8 is below threshold.

steps.message: Assessed all ten sealed discussion assignments against retained evidence and the recent-post index. Six concrete chores received scoped provisional plans and five criterion scores; all scored experiments are below the 6.0 threshold. The remaining four lack a supportable bounded chore or are a one-off authorization fault. No post proposed.
